deviations.what: merge t1 (Provider protocol tightening) after t4 and t5 land, instead of at the end of wave 1 — task execution order and all acceptance criteria are unchanged; only the merge point moves
deviations.reason: t1 adds write/stop to the runtime_checkable Provider protocol, but DockerProvider only satisfies it at t4 (wave 2) and t5 (wave 3). Merging t1 at the end of wave 1 makes test_provider_satisfies_the_protocol fail for the docker binding across two full waves, which violates assign-to-workforce's hard rule that tests pass after every merge. Deferring t1's merge keeps the protocol tightening simultaneous with the backends satisfying it, so the suite stays green at every merge point.

deviations.what: the main agent reconciles two signature divergences at merge time rather than re-dispatching the task agents: the digest keyword becomes expected_sha256 (t1 authored sha256) and the fake's stop() returns StopOutcome (t1 authored the dataclass, t3 returned None)
deviations.reason: t1 and t3 built the two halves of one seam concurrently in wave 1 and diverged on two names despite pinned briefs. expected_sha256 wins because it matches the established convention in core/artifacts.py::export_artifact; StopOutcome wins because a verb that reports what it found beats one that reports nothing. Reconciling at the merge point costs one small commit; re-dispatching both agents costs a wave.

deviations.what: serialize every test run that touches the live Docker engine: no merge gate runs while a task agent is running its suite, and Docker-heavy tasks are staggered rather than dispatched alongside a gate
deviations.reason: The t6 merge gate went red on two Docker tests that both pass in isolation, with no leaked engine resources; a re-run with the t4 agent quiescent gave 763 passed / 0 failed. Cause: t4's agent was running its own full suite against the same Docker daemon as the gate, and this project's live-engine tests use deterministic object names (headspace-<workspace_id>), so two concurrent suites collide on shared engine state. The plan's wave structure guarantees file-disjointness, which says nothing about a shared external resource — the daemon is a single global object every worktree reaches into, so 'parallel = serial' holds for the source tree and breaks for the engine.

deviations.what: honesty condition h6 is satisfied per-verb, not uniformly: 'headspace put' records path+sha256 in all four surfaces including outcome_summary, but 'run --input' deliberately summarises a copy-in by file count and total bytes in outcome_summary while still recording path+sha256 in provenance.inputs, the journal intent payload and state.json
deviations.reason: h6 as confirmed says the marker test yields an outcome_summary containing the file's path and sha256. A multi-file run --input cannot list every file's path and digest in a one-line summary without becoming the unbounded blob the result package exists to avoid, so _run_summary reports count and total bytes instead. The load-bearing half of c6/h6 — path and digest recorded, contents never — holds on every surface for both verbs; only the outcome_summary rendering differs, and t11 pinned that difference with an explicit assertion rather than switching verbs to make the test pass.

deviations.what: confirmed claim c43 ships half-met: the stop verb reports cancelled/exit 5 on every backend, but the stopped job's own recorded outcome on Docker stays failure/exit 137 and its run invocation exits 6 — tracked as issue #16, not silently absorbed
deviations.reason: The job's outcome is written by the concurrent run invocation from what its backend reports, and DockerProvider._status has no branch that can produce STATUS_CANCELLED. Verified live, not inferred. It is not a one-line fix: docker.py's own docstring establishes that exit 137 with OOMKilled false is indistinguishable from a job that deliberately exited 137, so the backend needs a cross-process discriminator that stop can set and run can read — and stop is engine-side-only by design (no lock, no state write), so that discriminator cannot be a state file. Choosing where it may live is a design decision that deserves its own change and its own live test rather than being improvised at the end of a large delivery. t8's tests pin the contract on the fake and none pretends Docker already meets it.
